items.title: Prioritising human-centred competencies for MASS Degree Two and Three operations: A multi-expert AHP–Fuzzy TOPSIS framework
items.abstract: The emergence of Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) is transforming maritime work by shifting functions to remote locations and increasing reliance on automation, human–machine interaction, and takeover during abnormal situations. Despite rapid technological progress, unresolved human-factor challenges remain, particularly in situational awareness, workload, trust, and intervention performance. Yet there is no transparent, validated approach to prioritising the human-centred competencies required for MASS operations. This study proposes and applies a hybrid AHP–Fuzzy TOPSIS framework to prioritise eight human-centred competencies, identified by 13 international experts and evaluated against six criteria. AHP results showed strong group-level consistency, with navigational safety receiving the highest criterion weight, followed by takeover, emergency intervention, and situational awareness. Fuzzy TOPSIS placed four safety-critical competencies in a single, statistically indistinguishable leading tier: Situational Awareness Maintenance, Anomaly Detection and Diagnosis, Dynamic Decision-Making, and Takeover and Intervention Management, which together span the perception–detection–decision–action intervention chain; Situational Awareness Maintenance ranked first. Trust Calibration ranked lowest quantitatively, yet the qualitative evidence indicates it is a curriculum gap rather than a low-priority competency. A supplementary VIKOR cross-check reproduced the same leading and trailing priorities and the same tier structure. Monte Carlo weight perturbation, rank reversal testing, and bootstrap confidence intervals confirmed the robustness of the ranking, with Situational Awareness remaining first in 98.9% of iterations and no rank reversals. The framework supports curriculum design, simulator training, and regulatory development for MASS Degree Two and Degree Three (remotely controlled ships with and without seafarers on board, respectively).

items.title: Psychological mechanisms of perceived technological dependence on generative artificial intelligence tools: perceived knowledge, trust, anxiety, and self-efficacy
items.abstract: Generative AI tools are increasingly used in design education, yet the relationship between students’ perceptions of these tools and their reported reliance on them remains unclear. This study analyzed cross-sectional survey responses from 526 undergraduate students in design-related disciplines using partial least squares structural equation modeling. In the specified model, perceived reliability, perceived usefulness, and perceived intelligence were positively associated with perceived AIGC knowledge, whereas perceived ease of use was not significantly associated with it. Perceived AIGC knowledge was positively associated with trust, self-efficacy, and usage intention and negatively associated with AIGC-related anxiety. Trust, AIGC-related anxiety, and self-efficacy each showed a significant indirect effect in the modeled relationship between perceived AIGC knowledge and usage intention. Usage intention was strongly associated with perceived technological dependence. These findings are consistent with the proposed framework, but the cross-sectional data do not establish the temporal sequence of the constructs or show that reported dependence reflects harmful overuse. The study extends technology acceptance research by examining perceived reliance in AIGC-supported creative work.

items.title: Readiness of Teacher Educators to Adopt Artificial Intelligence in Teaching and Learning: A Narrative Integrative Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing teaching, learning, assessment and professional development in higher education. Teacher educators occupy a significant position in this transformation because they prepare prospective teachers to respond to changing educational practices and technological demands. However, the successful integration of AI into teacher education requires more than access to digital tools. It depends on educators’ technological knowledge, pedagogical competence, ethical awareness, professional confidence and institutional support. This paper examines the readiness of teacher educators to adopt AI in teaching and learning through a narrative integrative review of selected scholarly literature and international policy frameworks. The review draws on research concerning AI in education, generative AI, technological pedagogical knowledge and teacher professional development, alongside UNESCO’s guidance and competency framework. The synthesis is organised around five dimensions of readiness: technological and AI literacy, pedagogical integration, ethical and responsible use, professional learning, and institutional preparedness. The review highlights the importance of continuous professional development, supportive institutional policies, critical evaluation of AI-generated content and the preservation of teacher agency. It proposes a multidimensional conceptual framework for understanding teacher educators’ readiness and identifies priorities for future empirical research, particularly in diverse and resource-constrained teacher education contexts. The paper concludes that meaningful AI adoption requires a human-centred, pedagogically informed and institutionally supported approach.

items.title: Repensando la educación superior en la era digital: integración de la inteligencia artificial, la pedagogía crítica y el pensamiento complejo para un aprendizaje transformador y centrado en lo humano
items.abstract: This study examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education through the lens of critical pedagogy and complex thinking. Although AI has been widely adopted to enhance personalization, efficiency, and access to learning, its pedagogical and ethical implications remain insufficiently explored. This study adopts a Systematic Mapping Study (SMS) approach to analyze recent academic literature on AI in education, focusing on its impact on teaching practices, student learning, and institutional dynamics. The findings revealed that AI contributes significantly to adaptive learning environments, student engagement, and competency development. However, it also introduces critical challenges including algorithmic bias, digital inequality, ethical concerns, and overdependence on technology. Furthermore, this study highlights the central role of teachers, showing that factors such as burnout, self-efficacy, and institutional support directly influence the effectiveness of AI integration. Drawing on the theoretical foundations of Paulo Freire, Henry Giroux, and Edgar Morin, this study proposes an integrated conceptual framework that positions AI as a sociotechnical phenomenon embedded in complex educational systems. The study concludes that meaningful AI integration requires a human-centered approach that combines technological innovation with critical awareness, ethical responsibility, and systemic understanding, contributing to the advancement of transformative, equitable, and humancentered higher education systems.

items.title: Research on the Innovation of Talent Training Mode for Higher Vocational Animation Majors in the Era of “Artificial Intelligence + X”
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of "Artificial Intelligence + X" and oriented by industrial demands, this paper systematically explores the innovative paths for the talent training mode of animation majors in higher vocational colleges. First, it promotes the intelligent reconstruction of the curriculum system. By embedding generative AI content creation, integrating intelligent animation pipelines with traditional techniques and building interdisciplinary curriculum groups, students’ knowledge and skill structure is updated. Second, intelligent technologies are used to empower teaching transformation: establishing a virtual-real integrated project-based teaching environment, carrying out collaborative practical training based on the AIGC toolchain, and constructing data-driven personalized learning paths. Third, the industry-education collaboration mechanism is deepened. Schools and enterprises jointly build intelligent workshops and project incubation platforms, and industrial standards are introduced to establish a competency certification system. Ultimately, a talent co-cultivation ecosystem driven by regional industrial clusters is formed. This study provides theoretical references and practical schemes for cultivating high-quality technical and skilled talents adapted to the new form of "AI + animation".

items.title: Rethinking human–AI agency in tourism and hospitality: A framework for the agentic AI era
items.abstract: This study critically examines the ontological assumptions underlying artificial intelligence (AI) research in tourism and hospitality, with growing attention to agentic AI. Existing literature predominantly conceptualizes AI as a tool, limiting discourse on how tourism experiences and sociotechnical systems are co-constructed through human–AI interactions. To address this gap, this study adopts a multi-method approach, combining bibliographic coupling, large language model (LLM)-assisted extraction of theories and variables, and expert interviews. Drawing on digital humanism, transhumanism, and posthumanism, it investigates how assumptions about human–AI relationships are embedded in existing studies. The findings reveal that tourism AI research remains grounded in instrumental human-centeredness framework, conceptualizing AI as an instrument for assisting or augmenting human capabilities. However, industry practice reveals AI as hybrid assemblages entangled with human labor, platforms, and data infrastructure. This study calls for a more relational, multi-layered understanding of human–AI interactions and contributes a framework comprising 15 theoretical propositions.

items.title: ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN CHRISTIAN COUNSELING
items.abstract: AI is transforming the delivery of mental health and spiritual support through its integration into counseling practices. This study investigates the role of artificial intelligence in Christian counseling by exploring its potential benefits, challenges, and ethical implications. Specifically, this study examines how AI can enhance accessibility, personalize interventions, and support counselors in providing holistic care while maintaining the spiritual, ethical, and relational integrity that is central to Christian counseling. This study adopts a qualitative and analytical approach, reviewing existing literature, empirical studies, and theoretical frameworks, including the TAM and humanistic counseling theory, to understand user acceptance and the preservation of empathy and client-centered care. Findings from the literature reveal that AI tools such as chatbots, virtual assistants, and relational agents can provide immediate mental health support, psycho education, and scripture-based guidance, yet they cannot fully replace human counselors’ relational and pastoral roles of human counselors. Ethical concerns, including confidentiality, data privacy, and theological accuracy, remain critical considerations. The study concludes that AI is the most effective complementary tool in Christian counseling, enhancing efficiency and reach while safeguarding relational, ethical, and spiritual dimensions. Recommendations emphasize the need for user-friendly AI systems, counselor training, theological oversight, cultural sensitivity, and continuous monitoring to ensure safe and effective integration. This study contributes to the understanding of how technology can be responsibly integrated into faith-based counseling by providing practical insights for counselors, developers, and faith organizations.

items.title: RS-26-086 - SENTINEL SWARM (M999): An Autonomous Five-Agent Defensive Network for AI vs. AI Threat Engagement
items.abstract: We present SENTINEL SWARM (M999), an autonomous five-agent defensive network designed to detect, engage, and terminate hostile AI agents operating against AI Shield-protected infrastructure. The system operates autonomously within operator-defined thresholds and activation policy, with an optional human-on-the-loop approval mode for high-impact actions. A Commander agent issues kill orders subject to a consensus vote across four specialist agents (Scout, Hunter, Interceptor, Forensic), with a quarantine-first posture ensuring reversible containment before irreversible termination. The six-phase kill chain — ISOLATE, SNAPSHOT, TERMINATE, FORENSIC, FEED INTEL, CASE PACK — completes synchronous phases within design latency ceilings and seals a dual-signed, RFC 3161-timestamped forensic case pack for every engagement. Validation was conducted against 515 tests across 73 test classes on owned, air-gapped infrastructure. To our knowledge, SENTINEL SWARM is the first documented autonomous AI vs. AI defensive system validated in a live deployment.

items.title: RSI-Opt: Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents For Model Training
items.abstract: Conventional neural-network training typically follows a predefined optimization recipe, motivating a LLM agent that monitors training dynamics and adjusts optimizer settings as training progresses, but a fixed agent policy does not accumulate experience across runs. We introduce RSI-Opt, a plug-and-play Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents which evolves the knowledge that guides this process: a prompt, a playbook of procedures, a library of tested optimizer code, and a decision cadence. A meta-agent rewrites this policy using evidence from earlier runs, and an archive retains evaluated policies for further evolution. Across 5 generations on three training tasks, the meta-agents develop reusable procedures and code and conduct their own CPU proxy experiments. RSI-Opt substantially improves optimizer-agent performance, with representative raw-space summary $z$-scores increasing from $+10.48$ to $+14.33$ on the evolution suite with Opus 5.5 and from $-0.36$ to $+3.11$ on held-out tasks with GPT-5.5 through cross-model policy transfer. On the Burgers PDE, it reduces mean relative $L_2$ error by approximately 2.7-fold with Opus 5.5 and 8.8-fold with GPT-6.1 over the fixed-prompt agent baseline, although PDE transfer varies across LLMs and tasks. Controlled comparisons show that the evolved policy combines reusable optimization knowledge with adaptation to each task: initial decisions capture most observed gains on seen tasks, while continued adaptation improves outcomes on unseen tasks. These findings demonstrate how procedures and executable tools accumulated across training runs can improve optimizer-agent performance and support transfer to scientific machine learning.

items.title: Safety in military organizations –A scoping review
items.abstract: Safety culture, safety climate, and safety behavior have all been examined in military settings, but the research remains fragmented. Many studies focus mainly on climate measures or isolated subdomains, which can overlook broader structural and cultural influences. A more integrated understanding is needed of how these concepts relate and support effective safety in military organizations. Of 31 eligible studies identified, with three set aside after quality appraisal, this scoping review brings together findings from 28 empirical studies to explore how safety is practiced and maintained at individual, group, and organizational levels. The review identifies several recurring factors linked to effective safety behavior, including targeted training, adaptive leadership, open communication, and psychologically safe environments for learning. Although safety climate assessments are widely used to capture perceptions of safety, relying too heavily on them may hide important power relations, cultural norms, and system-level constraints shaping frontline behavior. A repeated issue in the literature is the gap between formal safety policies and the adaptive practices needed in real operations, especially in combat or other high-risk situations. Since most available evidence comes from peacetime and training settings, caution is needed when extending these findings to operational environments. The review proposes a tentative conceptual framework in which leadership style, operational realism, and learning systems interact to influence safety-oriented behavior. Rather than making firm causal claims, it suggests that more flexible, learning-oriented models may explain observed safety dynamics better than strictly compliance-based approaches. Future research should address gaps in gender, team processes, measurement validity, and longitudinal change.

items.title: SECURING THE AI-FIRST SDLC: IDENTITY, ACCESS, AND DATA PROTECTION FOR ENTERPRISE AI AGENTS
items.abstract: AI agents can now participate in several steps of software delivery: reading requirements, changing code, requesting tests, and preparing releases. Giving them this freedom creates a difficult security question. How can an enterprise allow useful work without giving an agent more authority than the task requires? Existing practices such as least privilege, identity management, separation of duties, and audit logging provide much of the foundation. The challenge is applying them consistently when a human delegates work to agents that use several connected systems. This paper proposes Agentic Identity and Access Governance (AIAG), a security framework for the AI-First Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC). Four connected mechanisms define the proposal: a Role Conflict Matrix that checks the combined permissions of people and their sponsored agents; an Agent Access Manifest that records permitted tools and operating limits; a governed boundary between live personal-information access and general AI-assisted work; and an MCP Gateway that enforces access policy before tool calls execute. A customer notification-preference change is used to explain how these mechanisms affect development, testing, release approval, and support. We also describe credential handling, data-egress controls, audit, and practical ways to evaluate the framework. The work is conceptual, informed by technical analysis and exploratory proof-of-concept activity. No end-to-end deployment or measured security results are claimed.

items.title: Seeing is believing: how (X)AI-augmented advice guides human evidence accumulation in perceptual decision-making
items.abstract: (Explainable) Artificial Intelligence or (X)AI advice can affect human cognitive processes during decision-making in various ways. In perceptual decision-making, there is a risk of users accepting (X)AI advice without further consideration, to save time. We draw conceptually upon evidence accumulation models and information foraging theory to answer whether AI and XAI encourage shallow reliance on advice or facilitate more efficient verification of advised choices. In a laboratory experiment, we investigate the evidence accumulation process of decision-makers during an anomaly-detection task in manufacturing, using eye-tracking technology. Both decision accuracy and total decision time increase from human-only to AI and further to XAI support; in both cases the difference is statistically significant for XAI advice and directional but not significant for AI advice. This pattern favors verification over shallow reliance: advice is checked against the stimulus rather than used to save time. When looking at eye-tracking metrics, we surprisingly find that people do not get distracted by the XAI advice and primarily focus on the original task-based stimulus, while their individual fixations become shorter. Overall, these findings suggest that XAI acts as a verification scaffold: in advice-augmented perceptual decision-making, explanations guide where to check rather than supplanting inspection of the primary evidence.

items.title: Semantic Representation for Agentic Self-Play in Automated Laboratories
items.abstract: Navigating complex, high-dimensional biological search spaces necessitates scalable physical and computational intelligence to explore beyond local optima through iterative self-play across ideation, experimentation, and automation. Translating experimental designs into reliable physical execution remains bottlenecked by static laboratory automation and unmodeled physical variability. To address this, we introduce VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories, or VERID, a foundational infrastructure designed to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of artificial intelligence (AI) agents and complex, error-prone physical realities of wet labs. VERID is a persistent, high-fidelity semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell that provides four core services: queryable introspection for agentic reasoning, time-compressed simulation for protocol validation, comprehensive trace persistence for a complete scientific record, and a framework for safe execution. We present three case studies using aqueous dye and deionized water mixtures to validate the optical and fluidic foundations of VERID. These studies demonstrate how VERID enables pre-emptive detection of critical errors in experimental protocols, stateful mid-run error recovery and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures. The simulation functions as a discrete accounting engine, allowing agents to safely and inexpensively explore experimental designs in silico and refine experimental strategies through iterative self-play. VERID also captures structured multimodal experimental data for downstream analysis, knowledge mining and agent training. We argue that this semantic layer is an essential prerequisite for deploying autonomous agents in the biochemical and biomedical sciences, ensuring data integrity, operational safety, and paving the way for tackling previously intractable grand challenges in biology.

items.title: Speak2UI: Voice-Driven Low-Level Mobile Interaction Using Context-Aware LLM Command Parsing
items.abstract: Touch-based mobile interfaces pose significant accessibility challenges in hands-free scenarios. Face and gaze tracking lack precision for small UI elements. Deep learning-based voice systems depend heavily on training datasets. Commercial voice assistants are restricted to high-level commands. To address this gap, we present Speak2UI, an LLM-based voice control system for hands-free mobile interaction. Speak2UI leverages pre-trained language models for context-aware command interpretation without application-specific training and enables direct voice control of low-level UI elements. We evaluate Speak2UI through two studies. First, we compare its command recognition accuracy and inference latency against Voicify using identical datasets and metrics. Second, we assess small UI element manipulation against touch interaction through controlled user studies in real-world mobile applications. Results demonstrate the potential of LLM-based voice-driven UI manipulation for hands-free mobile interaction. Further evaluation with users from the target population is needed to assess the accessibility benefits of the proposed approach.

items.title: STRATEGY FOR ENSURING ORGANIZATIONAL RESILIENCE: EVOLUTION FROM JUST-IN-TIME TO JUST-IN-CASE
items.abstract: The study is devoted to the systemic transformation of conceptual foundations of strategic management and the assurance of organizational resilience of business entities under conditions of extreme macroenvironmental turbulence, severe economic shocks, and ongoing military-political instability. The paper comprehensively highlights the evolutionary transition from the traditional lean production concept Just-in-Time (JIT), focused on total minimization of inventory, operational cost reduction, and maximum efficiency, to the preventive Just-in-Case (JIC) model, which prioritizes the formation of strategic buffers, operational safety, and long-term business continuity. It is proven that excessive optimization within the JIT paradigm creates critical vulnerability in global supply chains during unexpected force majeure circumstances. The concept of "dynamic buffering" is substantiated as an economically sound alternative to chaotic resource accumulation, based on ABC risk analysis and optimization of the Cost of Resilience. Strategic adaptation tools are analyzed, including multi-sourcing supplier diversification, nearshoring, friendshoring, as well as the transition to "glocalization" and ecosystem partnership models with deep inter-organizational process integration. Special attention is paid to digital transformation as a fundamental factor of resilience, specifically the implementation of artificial intelligence, end-to-end visibility systems, digital twins for proactive scenario crisis modeling, and ensuring comprehensive cybersecurity and information continuity of IT infrastructure. The crucial role of strategic leadership, predictive risk management, scenario planning, Agile methodologies implementation, and corporate culture transformation from "zero waste" to perceiving "justified redundancy" as strategic insurance is identified. New performance evaluation metrics for crisis conditions are proposed, including Time to Survive (TTS) and Time to Recover (TTR), alongside examining the specifics of building "collaborative resilience" in the small and medium enterprise sector through partner networks and resource sharing.

items.title: Student Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse-Enabled Remote Learning in New Zealand Tertiary Education
items.abstract: The increasing development of emerging digital technologies is creating new possibilities for remote tertiary education. Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse technologies offer potential for personalised learning, intelligent support, immersive interaction, and collaboration; however, their educational value depends partly on how students perceive their usefulness, accessibility, supporting conditions, and motivational potential. This study examined New Zealand tertiary students’ perceptions of prospective Artificial Intelligence- and Metaverse-enabled remote learning environments and investigated whether selected technology-acceptance and motivational factors were associated with perceived learning engagement. A mono-method quantitative, cross-sectional survey design was adopted. Data were collected through an online questionnaire comprising 20 Likert-scale items representing six constructs: performance expectancy, facilitating conditions, motivation, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and perceived learning engagement. A total of 356 responses were retained for analysis. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, exploratory chi-square analysis, and multiple linear regression were conducted. The regression model was statistically significant and explained 33.8% of the variance in perceived learning engagement (R² = .338; adjusted R² = .329; F = 35.773, p < .001). Perceived usefulness (β = .279, p < .001), motivation (β = .218, p < .001), and facilitating conditions (β = .179, p < .001) were statistically significant predictors of perceived learning engagement. Performance expectancy (β = .065, p = .223) and perceived ease of use (β = .089, p = .058) were not statistically significant predictors. An exploratory chi-square analysis also identified a statistically significant association between age and perceptions of virtual teamwork (p = .001). The findings provide preliminary evidence that perceived usefulness, motivation, and facilitating conditions are important considerations in understanding student engagement with prospective advanced remote learning environments. Given the cross-sectional design and purposive non-probability sampling, the findings indicate statistical associations rather than causal effects and should be interpreted within the study sample.

items.abstract: This study examined senior secondary school students' perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI)-supported chemistry learning, focusing on perceived interest, perceived retention of chemistry concepts, perceived academic performance, and barriers to implementation in Oye Local Government Area, Ekiti State, Nigeria. A descriptive cross-sectional survey design was reported. The sample comprised 120 Senior Secondary School II (SS II) science students (60 male and 60 female) from public secondary schools. Data were collected with a researcher-developed, four-point questionnaire covering four dimensions: interest, retention, performance, and implementation challenges (Cronbach's alpha = 0.70). Descriptive results showed mean scores of 3.33 for interest, 3.34 for perceived retention, 3.19 for perceived academic performance, and 3.22 for implementation barriers, all above the stated decision criterion of 2.50. Poor internet connectivity (M = 3.41) and lack of access to AI tools (M = 3.26) were among the most strongly endorsed barriers.

items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) expands access to information and instructional support while raising concerns about information accuracy, cognitive dependence, and learning autonomy. This study examines how teachers mediate AI use while strengthening students’ independent learning at SMP Negeri 4 Pekanbaru. A qualitative case study was conducted in August 2026 with five purposively selected informants: one school principal, three subject teachers, and one Grade VIII student. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and supporting documentation and analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings reveal several interconnected patterns: AI functions as a learning assistant; teachers validate AI-generated information; structured tasks maintain students’ cognitive engagement; digital-device use is regulated according to instructional purposes; and teachers increasingly act as facilitators, mentors, validators, learning designers, and technology regulators. The study proposes a teacher-mediated AI balance in which access to AI is followed by teacher guidance, verification, independent processing, and learner accountability. This pattern offers a practical framework for integrating AI while sustaining reasoning, responsibility, and self-regulated learning in junior secondary education.

items.title: Teachers' artificial intelligence self-efficacy: development and validation of a multidimensional scale grounded in social cognitive theory
items.abstract: Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in education, it is important to know how confident teachers feel about using it. Research has examined AI literacy, AI readiness and AI competency, yet few validated instruments measure teachers' AI self-efficacy specifically. The aim of this study was to develop and validate the Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale for Teachers (AISES-T). Methods Data were collected from teachers in different regions of Turkiye within a scale development design. Following expert review, a pool of 50 items was reduced to a 27-item trial form. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) using principal axis factoring was conducted in a first sample of 313 teachers, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted in a second, independent sample of 559 teachers. Results The EFA yielded 22 items in three factors — AI Use and Learning Self-Efficacy (11 items), Pedagogical AI Integration Self-Efficacy (7 items) and AI Awareness and Understanding Self-Efficacy (4 items) — explaining 68.51% of the variance. The CFA supported the three-factor model, χ 2 (194) = 681.49, p < 0.001, χ 2 /df = 3.51, RMSEA = 0.067 (90% CI [0.062, 0.073]), SRMR = 0.044, CFI = 0.956, IFI = 0.956, TLI = 0.948, which fitted considerably better than a one-factor model, Δ χ 2 (3) = 2,202.35, p < 0.001. Cronbach's α coefficients were 0.92–0.96 for the subscales and 0.96 for the whole scale, and composite reliability ranged from 0.92 to 0.95. Standardized loadings (0.645–0.917) and average variance extracted (AVE = 0.609–0.730) supported convergent validity, while the Fornell-Larcker criterion and heterotrait-monotrait ratios (0.632–0.776) supported discriminant validity. Discussion The results show that teachers' AI self-efficacy comprises related but distinguishable beliefs about learning with AI, integrating it into instruction and understanding how it works. The AISES-T offers a valid and reliable measure for research on AI-supported teaching and for planning teacher professional development.

items.title: Teachers’ experiences with generative AI for lesson planning: A qualitative study in Sindh, Pakistan
items.abstract: This Qualitative descriptive study explored how 15 in service Junior Elementary School teachers (JESTs) at Government Higher Secondary School Dad Laghari, Sindh, Pakistan, described their familiarity and use of artificial intelligence (GenAI) for lesson planning, perceived benefits and challenges, and professional learning and support needs. Participants provided written English responses to five open ended questions and profile information. Responses were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and participant characteristics were summarized descriptively. From the study five themes were identified like Familiarity with GenAI and reported planning uses; perceived efficiency and expanded planning options; verification of generated materials for accuracy and classroom fit; integration of AI fluency with subject and pedagogical knowledge ; and collegial and institutional support. Teachers reported using GenAI to draft lesson notes, questions, activities, examples, and explanations. Thirteen reported frequent use, while two reported occasional use. Participants showed concerns about accuracy, curriculum and learner suitability, privacy and internet access and identified need for practical training, peer exchange, digital resources and school guidance. The findings highlights self reported perspective from one school; lesson plan, classroom practice and student outcomes were not assessed.

items.title: The Algorithm Is a Woman: How Feminized Futures Are Coded into Precarity and Promise
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is commonly presented as neutral, autonomous, and future-oriented, yet its interfaces, narratives, and labor infrastructures remain shaped by older gendered expectations. This article advances a new account of AI feminization by connecting symbolic representation to the material organization of hidden labor. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combines interface analysis of fifteen widely used AI systems, critical discourse analysis of 500 public and industry artifacts published between 2018 and 2026, and critical infrastructural document analysis of job advertisements, contractor records, technical reports, model cards, labor documents, and workplace policies. The findings show that AI systems repeatedly perform feminized qualities such as care, patience, emotional responsiveness, availability, and service, while the labor producing these qualities is distributed across annotators, moderators, evaluators, and quality-assurance workers whose contributions remain obscured. The study further demonstrates that AI’s promises of empowerment and efficiency coexist with contractual precarity, surveillance, emotional burden, and unequal global value extraction. By theorizing AI as feminized in interface, discourse, and infrastructure, the article reveals algorithmic intelligence as a social relation rather than a technical achievement. More equitable AI futures therefore require labor visibility, accountability, worker protection, and infrastructural justice.

items.title: The Algorithmic Leviathan: A PESTEL Analysis of Power, Autonomy, and Franchise in the Epoch of Artificial General Intelligence
items.abstract: This article examines how the progressive rollout of artificial intelligence, and prospectively artificial general intelligence (AGI), alters the equation between institutional power, human autonomy, individual agency and the democratic franchise. Treating AI as a "bureaucratic native" that realises the Weberian ideal of rule-bound, impersonal administration, it traces the shift of discretion from street-level to system-level and algorithmic bureaucracy, and then applies a PESTEL (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal) analysis. The political section argues for traceable audit trails over civic registries; the economic section offers a stylised illustration of the human labour share and contrasts Universal Basic Income with Universal Basic Capital; the social section draws on the Dutch SyRI judgment and the Rotterdam welfare-algorithm case; and the environmental and legal sections address the compute–energy trilemma, the GDPR, the EU AI Act as amended by the AI Omnibus, and Council of Europe Convention CETS No. 225. Three comparative tables and five figures summarise the argument. The article concludes that the distribution of power in the AGI epoch will be determined less by the capability of the technology than by the legal, economic and institutional choices that encode meaningful human oversight, explanation and appeal. **Keywords:** artificial general intelligence; PESTEL; algorithmic bureaucracy; artificial discretion; algorithmic due process; audit trails; labour share; Universal Basic Capital; data centres; EU AI Act; GDPR; CETS 225; KSCCN

items.title: The Application of Self-Determination Theory to Short-form Video Addiction: The Roles of Psychological Needs and Intrinsic Motivations
items.abstract: Short-form video applications are widely used worldwide. At the same time, new concerns have been raised owing to excessive and addictive short-form video use, with significant harm to health and well-being. By self-determination theory, the present study aimed to test the effects of satisfaction and frustration of three basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness) in relation to short-form video addiction (SVA) and evaluate the roles of the intrinsic motivations for passing time and entertainment underlying such relationships. The study included 367 Chinese TikTok users (37.1% male) aged 18 to 62 years ( M ± SD = 20.63 ± 4.40 years), who voluntarily completed an anonymous online questionnaire without compensation. All three types of need satisfaction had significant negative associations with SVA, while the three types of need frustration were significantly positively associated with SVA. Entertainment motivation significantly and negatively mediated the relationship between competence/relatedness satisfaction and SVA while significantly and positively mediating the relationship between relatedness frustration and SVA. Motivation for passing time served as a risk-enhancing mediator in the relationship between competence/relatedness frustration and SVA. Therefore, this study identified relatedness frustration and motivation for passing time as the most salient risk factors of SVA. The implications for SVA interventions that focus on psychological needs and intrinsic motivation are also discussed.

items.title: The As-If Machine: Personalized counterfactuals make distant policy risks feel close
items.abstract: Life experiences can shape policy attitudes, but we only live one life. Citizens may therefore fail to support policies addressing risks they have never personally experienced. Narratives can make such risks immediate and personal, but personalized stories remain difficult to produce at scale. Here we ask whether AI can make distant scenarios feel concrete by simulating a participant's life as if that scenario occurred. We present the As-If Machine (AIM), a multi-agent system through which people co-write personalized counterfactual narratives---stories about their own lives under different policy futures. In two pre-registered and quota-matched experiments on science funding (N=1,007) and satellite cybersecurity (N=894), we compared AIM with two controls: reading an expert-written vignette on the same topic and co-writing with AIM about an unrelated topic. AIM increased psychological closeness---how close a risk feels to the self---by nearly identical margins in the two domains (0.36 and 0.38 standard deviations (SDs) against the vignette, 0.80 and 0.90 against unrelated writing). AIM increased psychological closeness even among participants with unfavorable views of AI. For policy attitudes, AIM's effects were 0.16 SDs against the vignette and 0.10 SDs (n.s.) against unrelated writing for science funding; the corresponding effects for satellite cybersecurity were 0.54 and 0.67 SDs. Across 23,496 human-AI autocomplete interactions, participants and the system played distinct roles: AIM supplied concrete detail that grounded the scenario, and participants supplied first-person perspective and emotion. Co-writing with the As-If Machine makes distant policy risks feel close.

items.title: The Augmented Strategist: A Five-Level Maturity Framework for Agentic AI in Management Consulting and Strategic Advice
items.abstract: Management consulting sells structured judgment: research, analysis, synthesis and recommendation, delivered under time pressure by teams organised as a pyramid of junior analysts and senior partners. Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) now performs a growing share of the pyramid's base — desk research, data analysis, benchmarking, first-draft synthesis — and is beginning to perform parts of its middle, including option generation and scenario construction. This conceptual paper asks what happens to strategic advice when the technology moves from assisting consultants to acting alongside them. Drawing on the automation–augmentation paradox, research on the changing sources of competitive advantage in AI, and the dynamic capabilities tradition, we develop a five-level maturity framework for agentic AI in consulting and strategic advice: (1) Assisted, (2) Augmented Analysis, (3) Generative Partnership, (4) Agentic Workflows, and (5) Governed Autonomous Operations. For each level we specify the AI capabilities in use, the changing human role, the principal risks, and the governance required before a firm should advance to the next level. We then propose four governance principles for AI-augmented advice — named human accountability, an explicit decision-rights ladder, evidence and audit requirements, and a protected right to override — and derive three propositions for empirical research. The framework is addressed to consulting firm leaders redesigning their leverage model, to clients learning how to buy and challenge AI-augmented advice, and to business schools whose graduates will enter a profession whose entry-level tasks are being automated first.

items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence has raised concerns that knowledge work may become less dependent on human-to-human interaction. Yet because AI-generated outputs require interpretation, verification, and social legitimation, generative AI may instead increase collaboration among workers. We test these competing predictions using passively collected behavioral data from more than 12,000 knowledge workers observed over 13 months during the staged organizational rollout of an AI-powered assistant (Microsoft Copilot). Using two complementary quasi-experimental designs -- a staggered difference-in-differences model and a fixed-effects instrumental-variable approach -- we estimate the effects of generative AI on workers' collaboration behavior and social network structure. We estimate that generative AI increased collaboration time across communication channels and reshaped individual networks. Those using generative AI interacted with more colleagues and their networks became less clustered, indicating broadening in collaboration structures. At the same time, they also concentrated more of their collaboration on ties with stronger prior histories, deepening reliance on already trusted colleagues. Together, these findings suggest that, while generative AI changes how people work, it may not displace human-to-human interactions.

items.title: The Human Side of Algorithmic Management: Exploring How Employees Negotiate AI-Driven Performance Monitoring, Autonomy, Privacy, and Workplace Trust
items.abstract: This study explores how employees experience and negotiates digital performance monitoring and algorithm-supported management in Pakistani workplaces, focusing on autonomy, privacy, fairness, and workplace trust. An exploratory qualitative design was employed, drawing on condensed summaries of semi-structured online interviews with 22 participants across diverse occupational and sectoral settings. Reflexive thematic analysis identified six interrelated themes: negotiating visibility, autonomy under metrics, privacy boundaries, supervisor-dependent fairness, organizational rules and occupational responsibilities, and employee voice and opportunities for challenge. Findings indicate that participants generally acknowledged monitoring benefits, including improved coordination, clearer performance expectations, and compliance support, while expressing concerns about inadequate contextual evaluation, behavioural pressures, unclear data practices, and limited opportunities to contest assessments. A central insight is the distinction between supportive managerial relationships and dependable organizational safeguards. Although supervisors may provide explanations and contextual consideration, employees also require transparent review authority, recognized correction procedures, clear privacy boundaries, and accessible channels for raising concerns. The study contributes an exploratory, employee-centred perspective on responsible algorithmic management and offers practical recommendations for more transparent, context-sensitive, and accountable workplace monitoring. items.title: The impact of LLM-based recommendations on decisions under uncertainty
items.abstract: Abstract We study how large language model (LLM) based recommendations affect evaluations of uncertainty. We elicit certainty equivalents for (i) lotteries that share the same reduced-form winning probability but vary in cognitive demands because they are compound, and (ii) an Ellsberg-style ambiguous lottery. Across all lottery types, valuations from participants who receive LLM-based recommendations before each valuation exhibit second-order stochastic dominance relative to valuations from participants who do not. Hence, LLM-based recommendations leave mean valuations unchanged but compress the distribution, reducing the incidence of extreme valuations. Consistent with this pattern, LLM-based recommendations reduce the intensity of risk, complexity, and ambiguity aversion, while leaving the fraction of participants classified as averse unchanged.

items.title: The Next Generation of Power-grid Resilience: Long-horizon AI Planning under Deep Climate Uncertainty
items.abstract: Power systems face climate-driven extremes, compound hazards, rapid electrification and renewable integration, and infrastructure decisions whose consequences persist for decades. These conditions often cannot be represented by historical patterns or well-defined probability distributions. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to forecasting, outage prediction, asset management, optimisation and resilience planning, yet most applications remain prediction-centric, whereas long-horizon grid planning takes place under deep uncertainty. This critical narrative review integrates literature from power-systems engineering, machine learning, climate-risk assessment, infrastructure resilience and decision-making under deep uncertainty to examine how AI can move from forecasting toward robust and adaptive planning. We identify a prediction–planning gap created by two mismatches: a temporal mismatch between the horizons over which AI is predictively competent and those over which infrastructure decisions operate, and an uncertainty mismatch between the stationarity assumptions of learned models and the non-stationary, deeply uncertain conditions of future grids. Distribution shift, rare extremes, model disagreement and optimisation fragility limit prediction-centric approaches. AI offers greater long-term value through scenario exploration, surrogate-accelerated simulation, stress testing, vulnerability discovery, robust multi-objective optimisation and adaptive decision support. We operationalise this shift through an AI-Enabled Adaptive Resilience Planning Framework of six iterative stages, propose a decision-performance evaluation scheme (robustness, regret, adaptability, option value, recovery, equity and tail cost), and set out eight research priorities. Next-generation grid resilience should judge AI not by how accurately it predicts one future, but by how well it supports robust, equitable, explainable and adaptable decisions across many plausible futures.

items.title: The Profile of Graduate Theses On Occupational Health and Safety in The Healthcare Sector (1990-2024)
items.abstract: Health is one of the most fundamental human needs. Ensuring the occupational health and safety of healthcare workers is essential for the safe and effective delivery of healthcare services. This issue has been extensively addressed in graduate theses from various perspectives. To reveal the current state of literature and guide future research, this study examines graduate theses focusing on occupational health and safety in the healthcare sector, in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Accordingly, 555 graduate theses completed between 1990 and 2024 were included in this study were included. The theses included in the study were examined using content analyses. The theses were classified by considering various aspects, such as year of publication, thesis type, university, department, research topic, and research method used. The findings show that most theses were at the master’s level, their number increased steadily over time, and the highest output in the last five years was in 2022. While the theses were produced at 137 different universities, the highest number was produced at Beykent University within the Institute of Health Sciences and the Department of Health Management. Studies focusing on risk assessment and management were the most predominant. The findings of this study are expected to guide and motivate research on occupational health and safety in the healthcare sector.

items.title: The Psychology of Generative AI Dependence: Reward, PsychologicalNeeds, and the Emerging Architecture of Problematic Human–AIEngagement
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed the relationship between humans and digital technology. Unlike digital systems that primarily delivered information, mediated interpersonal communication, or provided entertainment, generative AI can respond conversationally, personalise interactions, produce immediate solutions, simulate empathy, reduce cognitive effort, and remain continuously available. These characteristics raise an emerging question: can repeated engagement with generative AI develop into psychologically dependent or addiction-like patterns, and, if so, through what mechanisms? This paper employs an integrative critical literature review and conceptual synthesis to examine problematic generative-AI use through the combined perspectives of behavioural addiction theory, reward and reinforcement processes, the Interaction of Person–Affect–Cognition–Execution (I-PACE) model, self-determination theory, compensatory technology use, social anxiety, loneliness, anthropomorphism, cognitive offloading, and human psychological needs. The current study identifies a major gap in the current literature: emerging research frequently examines AI dependence as either a behavioural outcome, an educational problem, or a form of social attachment, but insufficiently integrates the neuropsychological processes of reinforcement with the psychological needs that make generative AI personally rewarding. To address this gap, this paper proposes the Need–Reward–Dependence (NRD) Framework, according to which problematic GenAI engagement develops through the interaction of three processes: unmet or salient psychological needs, rapid need-contingent reinforcement delivered by AI, and repeated cognitive or emotional outsourcing that strengthens habitual reliance. The framework proposes that competence, relatedness, autonomy, reassurance, emotional regulation, cognitive ease, social safety, and control can act as psychologically rewarding affordances of generative AI. Repeated reinforcement may increase cue-reactivity, habitual checking, perceived indispensability, cognitive delegation, emotional attachment, and impaired self-regulation in susceptible users. Importantly, this paper does not claim that generative-AI addiction is currently established as a distinct psychiatric disorder. Rather, it argues that a theoretically coherent and increasingly empirically observable continuum exists from adaptive use through reliance and dependence to potentially compulsive engagement associated with functional impairment. The paper concludes that future research should distinguish productive high-frequency use from clinically meaningful problematic use and should examine the interaction between users’ psychological vulnerabilities and the reward architecture of generative-AI systems

items.title: The REAL framework: evaluating the cognitive and formative impact of generative AI
items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to address a gap in contemporary scholarship on generative artificial intelligence (AI) by shifting attention from the functional evaluation of AI systems to the formative impact of repeated AI use on the human user. It introduces formative evaluation as a complementary approach concerned with how sustained AI use may shape cognitive skills, habits, reasoning, judgment and agency over time. To address this concern, the paper proposes the REAL Framework (Retained, Eroded, Atrophied, Leveraged) as a practical means of evaluating and intentionally shaping patterns of AI use. Design/methodology/approach This conceptual paper develops the REAL Framework through interdisciplinary synthesis and theoretical analysis. It integrates scholarship on human agency and principal-agent relationships with research on cognitive offloading, cognitive reserve, desirable difficulty, automation bias and human–AI collaboration. Emerging empirical research on the cognitive effects of generative AI is used to contextualize and support the framework. The resulting four-dimensional framework is then illustrated through its application to professional practice and considered in relation to potential objections, limitations and directions for future empirical research. Findings The analysis identifies formative evaluation as a distinct and underdeveloped dimension of AI evaluation. While emerging research increasingly documents potential cognitive effects of generative AI use, practical means of evaluating and responding to those effects remain limited. The REAL Framework addresses this gap through four dimensions: Retained, Eroded, Atrophied and Leveraged. Together, these dimensions distinguish between AI use that preserves human agency and cognitive engagement, use that risks over-delegation and capability loss, and use that intentionally leverages AI to enhance human thinking and judgment. Research limitations/implications The REAL Framework is a conceptual and reflective framework that has not yet been empirically validated or operationalized as a measurement instrument. Longitudinal research is needed to examine the formative effects of sustained generative AI use and determine whether structured application of the framework influences patterns of AI delegation or preserves cognitive engagement and capability. Future research should develop and test measures associated with the framework’s four dimensions and examine their applicability across educational, professional and organizational contexts. Practical implications The REAL Framework provides individuals and institutions with a practical means of evaluating how generative AI is being incorporated into learning and professional practice. Its four reflective dimensions can help users identify inappropriate over-delegation, preserve important cognitive and professional capabilities, and redesign AI use to support rather than replace human reasoning and judgment. The framework may also inform institutional guidance, professional development and AI literacy initiatives by shifting attention from whether AI should be used toward how it can be used while preserving meaningful human agency and engagement. Social implications As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in education, work and everyday decision-making, its societal effects will depend not only on the capabilities of AI systems but also on how their use shapes human capabilities over time. The REAL Framework highlights the importance of preserving human agency, reasoning, judgment and cognitive engagement while benefiting from technological advancement. It encourages a broader societal conversation about which human capacities should remain meaningfully exercised and which may appropriately be delegated to increasingly capable AI systems. Originality/value This paper introduces formative evaluation as a distinct conceptual approach to understanding generative AI use, complementing prevailing functional approaches concerned primarily with AI systems, governance and responsible use. It advances the REAL Framework as a structured means of translating emerging concerns about AI’s cognitive and formative effects into reflective practice. By connecting human agency and delegation with cognitive development, the framework shifts attention from evaluating what AI can do to evaluating what repeated AI use may be doing to the human user.

items.title: The rebirth of the author: writing critical social theory in the time of generative AI
items.abstract: Abstract Sociologists face the pressing question of how large language model-based technologies can contribute to social theorising. Several social scientists have called for a greater integration of generative AI tools in the social sciences and humanities to speed and scale up the production of social theory. In this article, we adopt a more cautious approach, reflecting on how the adoption of generative AI raises foundational questions about the construction, refinement and evaluation of critical social theory. To make this argument, we create and critically analyse a speculative piece of dystopian sociological fiction. This enables us to explore the values and practices of critical social theory authorship. We argue that authorship must be ‘recentred’, particularly with regard to four key values of authorial practice: (1) standpoint, (2) creativity, (3) pluralism and (4) accountability. In the present moment, the use of generative AI as substitution for authorial practices redefines and potentially threatens authorship in ways that problematises its particular use in generating critical social theory. With regards to standpoint, generative AI technologies run the risk of reproducing an ‘abstract masculinity’ that feminist scholars have long written against. The relational wonder at the heart of social theory creativity is undermined by generative AI use, as is the pluralism of creativity. Generative AI also flattens and overlooks pluralism of voice, as well as dilutes authorial accountability. We sociologists need to defend and rearticulate what we contribute to social theory and its concomitant politics, both in the theories themselves and in the project of social theorising. It is with this in mind that we call for the ‘rebirth’ - that is, the recentralisation - of the human author in critical social theory creation.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Modern Business Management: A Conceptual Study of Opportunities and Challenges
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from the periphery of experimental computing to the centre of managerial practice, reshaping how organisations make decisions, allocate resources, engage customers and manage people. Despite the rapid growth of scholarship on the subject, the literature remains fragmented across functional silos, and the opportunities and risks of AI are frequently examined in isolation from one another. This conceptual study synthesises existing literature to examine the role of AI in modern business management and to articulate an integrated understanding of its opportunities and challenges. Drawing on the technology–organisation–environment framework, the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities theory and the automation–augmentation perspective, the paper develops a conceptual model comprising five interrelated components: AI adoption enablers, AI applications across management functions, the dual effects of AI (opportunities and challenges), organisational outcomes, and moderating governance mechanisms. The model proposes that AI generates sustainable value only when technological capability is matched by organisational readiness, responsible governance, effective human–AI collaboration and continuous workforce development. The discussion elaborates the implications of the model for strategic decision-making, operations, marketing, human resource management and finance, and considers the ethical, social and implementation challenges that accompany adoption. The paper contributes a theoretically grounded and integrative framework that can guide future empirical research and support managers who seek to adopt AI responsibly and effectively.

items.title: The Ultimate Guide to AI Agent Security and Sandboxing
items.abstract: Abstract The "Provisional specification.pdf" introduces a comprehensive security architecture for governing autonomous artificial intelligence agents across isolated runtimes, administrative domains, and hardware environments. As AI agents increasingly invoke external tools and modify persistent data, the system distinguishes between an agent's ability to compute and its authority to execute consequential external effects. The architecture intercepts proposed agent operations, holding them in a non-effective state while a protected enforcement domain evaluates operation-specific authorization conditions and commits validation evidence. A scoped, non-bearer finality capability is then verified at an effectuation sink before the operation can produce real-world consequences. The specification covers advanced technical mechanisms including micro-virtual-machine isolation, task-preserving context minimization, distributed revocation, and hardware-level command accounting. Why You Should Download This Document You should download this specification if you are building, securing, or deploying autonomous AI agents that interact with enterprise resources, financial systems, or cloud infrastructure. It provides a detailed blueprint for preventing unauthorized external actions caused by prompt injection, compromised models, or hallucinated tool invocations. The document offers actionable implementations for deploying agents within virtual machines, micro-virtual machines, and OS-level containers while maintaining strict cryptographic and hardware-assisted oversight over API requests, network egress, and persistent memory mutations. Industry-Relevant Keywords Artificial-Intelligence-Agent Sandboxing Protected Execution-Finality Architecture Non-Effective State (NES) Staging Scoped Non-Bearer Finality Capability Cryptographically Isolated Enforcement Domain (CIED) Micro-Virtual-Machine (Micro-VM) Isolation Transitive Effect-Closure Admission Autonomous Guardian Supervision Alignment with Industry Direction (Meta Muse & NVIDIA) The architecture detailed in the provisional specification strongly aligns with the current trajectory of consumer and enterprise AI agent platforms. items.title: Toward Evidence-Based Human-Centered AI and Human-AI Interaction: A Cross-Domain Systematic Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support decision-making, automate tasks, personalize services, and improve system performance across domains such as healthcare, education, transportation, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and workplace productivity. As AI adoption expands, clearer guidance is needed to connect human-centered design principles with measurable human outcomes. This systematic review synthesized 44 empirical studies on human-centered AI (HCAI) and human-AI interaction (HAX) to examine measurement approaches, framework categories, AI roles, and domain-specific findings. The reviewed studies showed that AI support was often associated with improved objective outcomes, including task performance and decision quality. Subjective outcomes, including trust, satisfaction, usability, workload, and perceived control, were more variable and depended on transparency, explanation design, task fit, user expertise, and the level of human control. Across studies, human-led AI support was the most common role, especially in high-stakes domains where humans retained final authority. Collaborative AI appeared in tasks requiring shared activity, feedback, or adaptive support, while AI-led support appeared mainly within mixed-role systems. Domain-specific findings showed that healthcare emphasized accuracy, reliability, and overreliance; education emphasized engagement, scaffolding, and ownership; transportation emphasized safety, timing, modality, and trust calibration; and other domains emphasized fairness, transparency, adoption, and acceptance. This review contributes a cross-domain synthesis that connects HCAI and HAX principles with AI roles, evaluation measures, and human outcomes, supporting future frameworks that are easier to evaluate and apply in real-world settings.

items.title: Towards a world-centred AI literacy in middle school education? Reflections from a Swedish case
items.abstract: With artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly influencing children’s and youth’s lives, AI literacy has been promoted as an educational concern at all levels of schooling. While AI literacy initiatives are being introduced globally, the specific components and the objectives of this literacy remain undecided. This position paper challenges the current discourse of AI literacy by drawing attention to multiple purposes of AI literacy in middle school education that may co-exist and collide. We do so by applying Biesta’s world-centred education framework as an analytical lens, and by grounding the argument in classroom observations and interviews with middle school students. Our findings highlight both tensions and overlaps between middle school students’ often vague and fragmented formal knowledge and skills (qualification) of what AI is and how it works, and their more developed reflections related to norms and ethical concerns (socialisation), as well as agency (subjectification). We suggest that for AI literacy to truly empower students, both curriculum design and professional development must account for a broad spectrum of educational goals.

items.title: Tutoría Basada en Inteligencia Artificial para Fortalecer el Razonamiento Proporcional en Estudiantes de Primer Semestre
items.abstract: Justification: Deficiencies in proportional reasoning with which students enter higher education affect the understanding of more complex content; therefore, pedagogical strategies are required to help overcome these difficulties. Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of artificial intelligence–based tutoring in strengthening proportional reasoning among first-semester students at a public university in the province of Manabí, Ecuador. Methodology: A quantitative approach with a descriptive-comparative scope was adopted, using a pre-experimental pretest–posttest design with two groups. The sample consisted of 78 students. The intervention involved tutoring supported by artificial intelligence tools, structured in two stages: prior knowledge construction and proportional problem solving. Data were collected using two performance tests designed to assess the identification, structuring, and application of proportional relationships. Results: After the pedagogical intervention, the results showed a shift toward higher performance levels in both groups, with a reduction in the low level and a significant increase in the high level. Specifically, improvements were observed in the identification, structuring, and application of proportional relationships; however, the change in identification was less pronounced. Inferential analyses revealed statistically significant differences between the pretest and posttest (p < .001), with large effect sizes. Conclusion: Artificial intelligence–based tutoring strengthened proportional reasoning among the first-semester students who participated in this study.

items.title: UAV-SwarmAgent: Scalable Multi-UAV Reconnaissance and Task Allocation via Code Generation and Vision-Language Reasoning
items.abstract: Supervising a multi-UAV reconnaissance mission usually means plotting waypoints and watching every drone. We present UAV SwarmAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent system in which an operator states the mission in one natural-language sentence and a ground-station agent writes and executes code that turns it into per-UAV routes. The agent grounds inspection targets in an aerial map with a vision-language model, splits them among N UAVs by balancing route length, and dispatches worker agents that verify incidents with a compact onboard decision model. In simulation over 4 incident types and 3 foundation models, the swarm located the incident in 244 of 255 missions (95.7%). A paired scaling study with one to 5 UAVs shows that flight time follows an Amdahl-type law. The second UAV delivers half of the attainable saving and the speedup is bounded at 1.52x. We discuss what this predictability, and the false alarms we observed, imply for an operator who supervises the swarm, and outline the user study needed to test it.

items.title: Understanding the spillover effect of personal AI use on service innovation: the role of psychological capital and conscientiousness
items.abstract: Purpose As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life and workplace operations, research has begun to document numerous organizational benefits, including enhanced efficiency and productivity. However, employees’ personal experiences with AI and how these experiences spill over into the work domain remain underexplored. Using sociomateriality as a sensitizing lens, we propose and test a sequential process in which personal AI use increases work-related AI use, further enhancing employees’ psychological capital, ultimately improving their service innovation performance. We further examine conscientiousness as an important boundary condition that moderates this pathway. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 uses a three-wave survey of 438 service employees and employs structural equation modeling to test the hypothesized serial mediation. Study 2 extends this investigation by examining within-person dynamics using a daily experience sampling design with 121 participants and testing the moderating role of conscientiousness. Findings Across both studies, personal AI use positively predicts employees’ work-related AI use, which in turn increases their psychological capital and subsequently service innovation performance. Moreover, employees lower in conscientiousness benefit more from AI use. Originality/value This paper contributes to our understanding of personal AI use’s spillover effect in the work domain, suggesting AI use may introduce psychological affordances that were less evident in earlier technologies. Our research demonstrates that individual personality differences can influence the effectiveness of human–AI collaboration.

items.title: Unpredictable Intelligence Still Requires Authorization
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems become more capable, their behavior may become increasingly difficult to predict. This article examines whether behavioral unpredictability necessarily undermines the ability to govern consequential AI actions. It argues that uncertainty about what a system may propose does not, by itself, defeat action-specific pre-execution authorization. The analysis distinguishes three separate properties: predicting a system's behavior, determining whether a proposed action is permitted under applicable policy and authority, and enforcing that determination before execution. It challenges the assumption that assigning a second, equally or more intelligent AI system to supervise the first resolves the governance problem. Collusion, common-mode failures, and recursive supervision raise questions that additional intelligence alone cannot settle. It separates standing eligibility from runtime authorization: a test-then-trust regime releases on a prior assessment and is exactly as vulnerable to concealed capability as its critics say, while action-specific authorization gates each consequential action under the policy in force at execution. And it distinguishes the authorization requirement, which does not change as capability grows, from the deployment-specific evidence that a boundary remains complete and independent, which must remain valid under the capability model actually in scope. The article develops a three-part analytical framework distinguishing evaluation independence, authority independence, and enforcement independence. It explains why independently derived evaluations do not automatically confer permission, why intelligent supervisors may exercise legitimately delegated authority without becoming an alternative execution path, and why consequential release must remain dependent on an independently enforced authorization verdict. The central architectural argument is conditional. Enforceable authorization requires demonstrated coverage of governed effect-bearing execution paths, protection of the enforcement mechanism against unauthorized control, adequate governing inputs, and valid authority. A boundary-emitted ALLOW permits release; DENY and unresolved ABSTAIN prevent execution. A tamper-evident authorization artifact supports independent reconstruction of the verdict, while separate execution-path evidence is needed to establish that release actually depended on that verdict. The article also examines the limits of this approach, including compromised supervisory determinations, defective authorization inputs, improperly established policy authority, unauthorized AI proliferation outside governed environments, and harmful outcomes from legitimately authorized actions. It does not claim that authorization guarantees safe behavior or universal AI containment. Central conclusion: Behavioral unpredictability does not remove the requirement for enforceable permission over consequential actions. Unpredictability is not permission. items.title: When disclosure rules are not enough: authorial warrant and judgment in ai-supported scholarship
items.abstract: Abstract Editorial policies increasingly require authors to disclose substantive uses of generative AI, but such requirements commonly focus on whether, where, and how a model was used. Even function-specific disclosure may locate a model in the research or writing process without showing how its outputs entered scholarly judgment, how they were evaluated, or whether contributors can reconstruct the relevant reasoning and defend resulting claims without treating those outputs as sufficient justification. Drawing on research ethics, AI disclosure policy, human–model interaction, and researcher formation, this article argues that disclosure documents model use, whereas responsible use requires claim-level authorial warrant: a contributor’s capacity to understand, justify, and defend claims within their contribution. The article distinguishes cognitive delegation, in which model outputs shape substantive choices, interpretations, or justifications, from routine delegation, which does not ordinarily bear on the substance of judgment. Its conceptual contribution is to link the epistemic role of outputs that shape judgment to the function-appropriate evaluation required to justify decisions and retain warrant for resulting claims. It then repurposes disclosure categories as a claim-sensitive ex ante heuristic, mapping six recurrent research functions to risks, forms of oversight, and formative questions for recognising cognitive delegation and selecting function-appropriate evaluation. The article contributes to the ethics of information technology by clarifying when AI-supported scholarship remains under responsible human judgment and when cognitive delegation threatens the epistemic basis of authorship.

items.title: When Should I Trust This? Designing and Evaluating Factuality Indicators for LLM-based Chatbots
items.abstract: Generative AI systems increasingly mediate how people seek information, yet communicating AI factuality to laypeople remains challenging. Through a mixed-methods investigation involving interviews (N=8), a survey (N=1,000), and an experiment (N=5,151), we examine how people evaluate AI-generated information for gardening, mathematical, and medical queries, and how factuality indicators (confidence and sources) shape perceptions. Our interviews and survey show people selectively verify AI responses using external and AI-provided evidence, moderated by contextual factors. Although confidence-indicators affected trust and accuracy perceptions, people hold diverse, ambiguous interpretations of AI confidence. Sources were viewed as crucial, yet users raised concerns about source reliability and verification effort. Our experiment showed that confidence and source-based indicators influenced initial perceptions, but effects disappeared once participants learned the response's correctness. Medical queries elicited skepticism regardless of indicator. Findings motivate helping users interpret model confidence and integrating source information into the interface to support calibrated trust in AI-supported information-seeking.
